title: The Psychology, Geography, and Architecture of Horror: How Places Creep Us Out
research_question: Why do some types of settings and some combinations of sensory information induce a sense of dread in humans? How do architecture, isolation, association with death, and other environmental qualities contribute to the experience of creepiness and dread?

participants.description: 1,029 females, 312 males, ranging in age from 18 to 77 (mean age of 28.97). Respondents from 54 different nations, with Americans being the largest group.
participants.recruitment: Online survey using an identical recruitment strategy as an unrelated study.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Hypothetical scenarios and descriptions: 44 different behaviors of a 'creepy person', 21 different occupations, 2 hobbies, and 15 statements about the nature of creepy people.

measures.instrument: Likert-type scales for likelihood, creepiness rating, and agreement with statements.
Likert-type scale (implied by agreement with statements)

findings.antecedent: Nonnormative nonverbal and emotional behaviors, unusual physical characteristics, unusual hobbies, or suspect occupations
findings.consequent: Activation of 'creepiness detectors'
findings.mechanism: Ambiguity of threat (difficulty understanding intentions, not knowing what to expect).
findings.quote: Nonnormative nonverbal, and emotional behaviors, unusual physical characteristics and hobbies, or suspect occupations set off our “creepiness detectors.”

findings.antecedent: Being male
findings.consequent: Likelihood of being perceived as creepy (by males and females)
findings.quote: Men were more likely to be perceived as creepy by males and females alike

findings.antecedent: Being female
findings.consequent: Perception of sexual threat from creepy people
findings.quote: women were more likely to perceive sexual threat from creepy people.

findings.antecedent: Uncertainty about a person's trustworthiness
findings.consequent: Judgment of creepiness
findings.mechanism: Ambiguity of threat.
findings.quote: uncertainty about whether the person was trustworthy or not was a key ingredient.

findings.antecedent: Physical characteristics (unusually lean body type, unusual facial features, especially eyes/teeth)
findings.consequent: Predisposition toward making a judgment of creepiness
findings.quote: physical characteristics such as an unusually lean body type and unusual facial features, especially in the region of the eyes or teeth, predisposed their participants toward making a judgment of creepiness.

findings.antecedent: Judgments of creepiness
findings.consequent: Occurrence as intuitive, relying on emotional reasoning rather than deliberative cognitive analysis
findings.quote: judgments of creepiness occurred, indicating that such judgments are intuitive and rely on emotional reasoning rather than deliberative detailed cognitive analysis.

findings.antecedent: Places offering a lot of prospect (clear, unobstructed view) and a lot of refuge (secure, protected place to hide)
findings.consequent: Attractiveness to humans
findings.mechanism: Evolutionary benefit for survival ('you can see without being seen, and eat without being eaten').
findings.quote: Attractive places offer us a lot of prospect and a lot of refuge, or what landscape architect Randolph Hester (1979) refers to as a “Womb with a View.”

findings.antecedent: Places offering very little prospect and very little refuge
findings.consequent: Perception as unsafe and dangerous
findings.mechanism: Lack of hiding places for self, many hiding places for potential threats.
findings.quote: places that offer bad combinations of prospect and refuge for us are perceived as unsafe and dangerous (Fisher and Nasar 1992)

findings.antecedent: More legible places (easy to recognize, organize into a pattern, recall)
findings.consequent: Preference
findings.mechanism: Ease of navigation and understanding.
findings.quote: More legible places are usually preferred over less legible ones

findings.antecedent: Sense of mystery (place contains more information than can be seen, inviting exploration) without potential danger
findings.consequent: Attractiveness of natural environments
findings.mechanism: Provides opportunity for learning and exploration.
findings.quote: a sense of mystery can increase the attractiveness of natural environments (Kaplan and Kaplan 1989).

findings.antecedent: Heightened sense of mystery accompanied by a sense of potential danger (e.g., deep narrow canyons, dark urban alleys, haunted houses)
findings.consequent: Attractiveness of the place
findings.mechanism: Potential danger overrides positive effect of mystery.
findings.quote: when a heightened sense of mystery is accompanied by a sense of potential danger... mystery decreases the attractiveness of the place

findings.antecedent: Bodies of water (deep water, rivers, lakes, ponds)
findings.consequent: Link with paranormal experiences (haunted highways, wells, ships, bridges)
findings.mechanism: Water poses a hazard to humans (drowning) and is a common cause of death, leading to associations with danger and the unknown.
findings.quote: bodies of water are frequently linked with paranormal experiences, as in the stories of haunted highways, ponds, wells, ships, and bridges detailed by Davies (2007) and Nickell (2012).

findings.antecedent: Being alone for extended periods, especially in uncertain environments
findings.consequent: Aversion, increased anxiety, hindered coping, increased perception of creepiness
findings.mechanism: Lack of emotional support and comradeship, difficulty resolving ambiguity, reliance on others for cooperative defense.
findings.quote: most people have an aversion to being alone for extended periods of time, especially in uncertain environments. Therefore, everything seems creepier to us when we are alone.

findings.antecedent: Being alone in an unusual environment
findings.consequent: Change in sensory information processing (attention turns inward, loss of confidence in understanding surroundings)
findings.mechanism: Monotonous or tedious stimulation causes attention to turn inward, leading to difficulty resolving ambiguity without social input.
findings.quote: When we are alone in an unusual environment, the way in which we process sensory information can change (Suedfeld 1987).

findings.antecedent: Large old buildings with rotting wood, exposed ductwork, and other structural defects
findings.consequent: Production of infrasound, increased creepy experience
findings.mechanism: Infrasound (low frequency sounds < 20 Hz) causes slight vibrations, registering as an unidentifiable, ambiguous signal that sets off creep detectors.
findings.quote: large old buildings full of rotting wood, exposed ductwork, and other structural defects can produce infrasound and make what is already a creepy experience even spookier.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to infrasound (low frequency sounds < 20 Hz)
findings.consequent: Sleeplessness, nausea, uneasiness, chills
findings.mechanism: Direct physiological/perceptual effect of infrasound.
findings.quote: In some people, the Hum can produce sleeplessness and even nausea. Two British scientists conducted an experiment on the Hum at a concert in London in 2003 (described by Lallanilla 2013)... resulting in widespread reports of uneasiness and chills from the concert-goers, and scientists have found the same effects under controlled laboratory conditions (Persinger 2001).

findings.antecedent: Typical Hollywood haunted house (darkness, confusing layout, hedges, iron fences, crumbling stairways)
findings.consequent: Difficulty fleeing, limited opportunities for escape
findings.mechanism: Architectural features impede movement and orientation.
findings.quote: the typical Hollywood haunted house is our worst nightmare as it makes fleeing difficult. The darkness and confusing layout of the house may cause us to get lost; at the very least, it would slow us down.

findings.antecedent: Being seated vs. standing, being in a corner vs. center, low ceilings
findings.consequent: Need for personal space
findings.mechanism: Feeling uncomfortable when personal space is violated, especially if escape is difficult.
findings.quote: we need more personal space while seated than while standing, more space when we are in the corner of a room rather than in the center of it, and more space in rooms with low ceilings (McAndrew 1993).

findings.antecedent: Haunted houses (typical portrayal: large, dark, overgrown vegetation, secret rooms, closets, attics, basements)
findings.consequent: Bad combination of very low prospect (for occupants) and very high refuge (for creepy things)
findings.mechanism: Provides hiding places for threats, limits clear views for occupants.
findings.quote: most haunted houses make for the bad combination of very low prospect for us, and very high refuge for the creepy-crawly things that are lying in wait to get us.

findings.antecedent: Older places
findings.consequent: Increased likelihood of being perceived as haunted
findings.mechanism: More time for tragic events to have occurred, leading to associations with death/trouble.
findings.quote: One of the main reasons why we think that older places are more likely to be haunted is simply because there has been much more time for tragic things to have taken place.

findings.antecedent: Stimuli associated with age (moldy odors, antiquated Victorian/Gothic architecture, wood interiors, old portraits)
findings.consequent: Increased creepiness of a place
findings.mechanism: Reinforces an ambiance of great age, priming associations with past tragic events.
findings.quote: stimuli such as moldy odors, antiquated Victorian or Gothic architecture, wood interiors, and old portraits on the wall reinforce an ambiance of great age and make a place seem creepier.

findings.antecedent: Malevolent spirits of deceased evil-doers
findings.consequent: Conceptualization as existing in 'trapped immortality' within highly circumscribed surroundings (dense forest, haunted house, single room)
findings.mechanism: Reflects evolved agent detection mechanisms and fear of danger in such environments.
findings.quote: The malevolent spirits of deceased evil-doers, on the other hand, are most easily conceptualized in a "trapped immortality” where they exist in highly circumscribed surroundings such as a particularly dense forest, a haunted house, or even a single room.

findings.antecedent: Signs of life suddenly interrupted and frozen in time (e.g., half-eaten meal, clothing laid out, abandoned city)
findings.consequent: Amplified fear factor, frightening ambiguity
findings.mechanism: Creates uncertainty about what took place, activating agent detection.
findings.quote: signs of life suddenly interrupted and frozen in time only amplify the fear factor; remnants of a half-eaten meal on a kitchen table or clothing laid out on a bed waiting for a home-owner who has apparently vanished without warning create a frightening ambiguity about what may have taken place in the house.

findings.antecedent: Places that isolate people without their consent (prisons, insane asylums, orphanages, hospitals)
findings.consequent: Perception as scary, increased likelihood of being considered haunted
findings.mechanism: 'Contamination' by association with troubled populations and bad events.
findings.quote: places that isolate people without their consent such as prisons and insane asylums are often considered scary. I would take this one step further and propose that any institution that once housed any "troubled" population of people may become “contaminated" by this association in the minds of imaginative individuals and thereby be believed to more likely to visit trouble upon visitors who dare to explore such places.

findings.antecedent: Death
findings.consequent: Perception as inherently creepy
findings.mechanism: Ambiguity surrounding death (when/how one will die, what happens after death).
findings.quote: Death is inherently creepy to us because of its ambiguity, and ambiguity is the soil in which horror grows.

findings.antecedent: Contemplating death
findings.consequent: Confusion and uncertainty, increased creepy mystique
findings.mechanism: Lack of evolved mental machinery to think of oneself as being dead.
findings.quote: the mere act of contemplating death is fraught with confusion and uncertainty, adding to its creepy mystique.

findings.antecedent: Places defined by death (e.g., graveyards, execution sites, battlefields, mines)
findings.consequent: Priming thoughts of one's own mortality, increased urgency in agent detectors
findings.mechanism: Direct association with death.
findings.quote: By priming thoughts of death, places defined by death quite naturally cause us to become aware of our own mortality, which may inspire a sense of urgency in our agent detectors.

findings.antecedent: Places that have been the scene of a death
findings.consequent: Increased likelihood of becoming haunted places
findings.mechanism: Longstanding unease around places associated with death.
findings.quote: places that have been the scene of a death frequently become haunted places

findings.antecedent: More gruesome and traumatic death
findings.consequent: Increased likelihood of the place where it happened becoming tainted by the event
findings.mechanism: Emotional impact of the event.
findings.quote: The more gruesome and traumatic a death, the more likely it is that the place where it happened becomes tainted by the event.

findings.antecedent: Suicide occurrence without additional creepy qualities
findings.consequent: Perception of a place as dreadful
findings.mechanism: The mere occurrence of suicide is not enough to make a place dreadful; additional qualities are needed.
findings.quote: the mere occurrence of a suicide does not seem to be enough in and of itself to make a place seem dreadful—the site must possess additional qualities to bestow true creepiness upon the locale.

findings.antecedent: Aokigahara Jukai forest (densely packed trees, rotting logs, moss, underbrush, lack of legibility, compasses not working due to magnetic iron)
findings.consequent: Perception as creepy
findings.mechanism: Combination of physical features that impede navigation and create ambiguity.
findings.quote: Unlike the Golden Gate Bridge, the forest has all of the trappings essential for being creepy. It is full of densely packed trees, rotting logs, moss, and underbrush, and the lack of legibility in the forest is exacerbated by the fact that compasses do not work there because of the high concentration of magnetic iron in the rocky volcanic soil.

findings.antecedent: Desecration or disturbing of graves/burial plots (e.g., construction projects, body snatching)
findings.consequent: Increase in strange paranormal activity around the graveyard
findings.mechanism: Disruption of the resting dead.
findings.quote: a disruption of burial plots by construction projects or body snatching invariably leads to an increase in strange paranormal activity around the graveyard.

findings.antecedent: Belief that a house is haunted, combined with self-confirming top-down processing guided by expectations
findings.consequent: Resolution of ambiguity in the direction of fear, perception of ghosts
findings.mechanism: Expectations drive perception, resolving ambiguous sensory information in line with existing fears.
findings.quote: They fed each other's fears by engaging in self-confirming top-down processing guided by expectations. Once they believed that their house was haunted, any ambiguity that they experienced was resolved in the direction that was dictated by their fears, which in this case meant that there were ghosts running wild in the house.

mechanisms: Ambiguity of threat: Difficulty understanding intentions or what to expect from a person or place.
Agent detection mechanisms: Evolved processes to protect from harm by predators/enemies, leading to hypervigilance.
Prospect-Refuge theory: Places offering clear views and secure hiding spots are preferred; lack thereof induces fear.
Legibility/Mystery: Ease of navigation and understanding; mystery can be attractive unless combined with danger.
Social isolation: Reduces ability to resolve ambiguity and cope with threat, amplifying creepiness.
Infrasound: Low-frequency sounds cause physiological and psychological discomfort, acting as an ambiguous threat signal.
Top-down processing: Expectations and beliefs influence perception, resolving ambiguous sensory input in line with existing schemas/fears.
Association with death/trouble: Places with a history of tragic events prime thoughts of mortality and activate threat detection.
moderators: Sense of potential danger (for the effect of mystery on attractiveness).
Additional creepy qualities (for the effect of suicide on dreadfulness).
